newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ watchdog ups vigilance of electricity sector.
newsitem.headline: NZ watchdog ups vigilance of electricity sector.

text.p: New Zealand's anti-monopolies Commerce Commission on Wednesday said the 'honeymoon period" was over for power companies and it would now increase its enforcement activity in the electricity sector.

"This year the Commerce Commission has given several energy companies warnings about conduct that could contravene the Commerce Act," Commission chairman Alan Bollard told the Electricity Supply Asoociation annual general meeting in Wellington.
He said that as a result, those companies had altered their behaviour, but warned that stronger action would be taken if necessary.

"The commission has now moved to the position where persistently anti-competitive behaviour may have to be taken to court. It is currently investigating the access pricing conduct of one power company, and has received complaints about a second sufficiently serious to warrant investigation," Bollard said.
He said the commission's main concern was with the way companies owning a local power network allowed, or obstructed, competitors' access to the network.

Deregulation of New Zealand's electricity industry has allowed power companies to sell electricity to customers anywhere in the country, but to do so they must have access to the networks owned by others.
"Typically this would be through a use of system contract or a conveyancy contract," said Bollard.

He said the Privy Council's decision in the Telecom v Clear court case spelt out that the owners of a network cannot insist, against the wishes of the customer, on the type of contract because in a normal competitive market they would lose the business to a competitor.
"Insistence on a particular form of contract could breach the Act," he said.
With deregulation, a system requiring all companies owning electricity networks to publicly disclose economic information about the networks, which are natural monopolies, was put in place.
Bollard said the commission had analysed the first year's data and was now awaiting the second year's information.
"It will be analysing this with some urgency and comparing the results with year one. It will then identify companies for its further attention," Bollard said.
He said the commission would not shrink from taking relatively heavy handed and expensive action through the courts where it considered it necessary.
